Yes.

**Explanation:** 
At the end of the story, Ilse makes a sudden shift that is both surprising and appropriate. Throughout the text, she acts guarded, stoic, and almost dismissive toward her son Jonas, even initially agreeing to leave him waiting alone on the dock while she takes the ferry across ("Kannst du"). This makes her last-second decision to turn around and invite him aboard surprising—not only to the reader, but to Jonas himself, who looks at her "without understanding." 

At the same time, this turn is completely appropriate in hindsight. Just before boarding, Ilse experiences a flood of memories about her late husband, Henning, the worn-down state of the ferry, and Jonas’s early childhood on those very planks. Furthermore, she doesn't break character by becoming suddenly overly sentimental; instead, she bridges the distance between them in the only language she knows—shared, practical labor ("Du kannst die Rampe machen"). This makes her change of heart feel deeply earned, coherent, and true to her character.
